object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged occurrence of something breaking, tracked through states from triage to closed.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, format INC- plus sequence, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence. ... Unique. And we never delete incidents

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform (or a manual alert raised by an engineer) indicating a possible issue.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket, potentially linked to an incident as its origin.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a ticket, in the support ticketing system's own format.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact / blast radius classification of an incident, SEV1 (everything down) through SEV4 (cosmetic/degraded).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer-urgency classification of an incident, P1 through P4, independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. ... Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Commander
object_types.definition: A named person who runs a declared incident for its duration; a role, not a job title.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system or capability owned by a team; incidents affect one or more services.

object_types.definition: Unique name of a service, enforced in the service catalogue.

ambiguities.description: Commander is identified only by name in the transcript ('One person, named'). Is name a reliable unique identifier, or does the Commander correspond to an existing Person/Employee entity with its own employee ID elsewhere in the org? Using name as reference_mode risks collisions.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' status mentioned by Owen is explicitly rejected as a formal state by Nadia and the facilitator, but Owen insists people treat it as one. Should an informal/interim status be captured as metadata even though it's excluded from the formal state model, to avoid loss of information used informally by staff?

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are described as changing over time ('Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius'), with history kept 'in the timeline, as events,' but the timeline/events concept itself is not modeled as an object type or fact type in this transcript. Should a Timeline/Event entity be introduced to capture severity/priority/state history, or is only the current-state snapshot in scope?

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The classification of incidents caused by customer misconfiguration (vs. genuine reliability events) was explicitly discussed but left undecided and deferred to Ravi. No cause-classification object type or fact type should be modeled, but this is a known gap in the current model that stakeholders flagged as important.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? ... Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are modeled as value types with a fixed enumerated set (SEV1-4, P1-4), but they are also revisable/mutable per incident over time; it's unclear whether these should instead be modeled as reference/lookup entity types (e.g., SeverityLevel entity) if additional attributes (like formal definitions of blast radius bands) need to be tracked separately from the incident.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. ... And priority is P1 through P4.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between an Incident and its origin (Alert/Ticket) is described as disjunctive-mandatory (at least one, possibly both), but it's unclear whether an Incident can have multiple Alerts or multiple Tickets as origins (the transcript mentions 'support gets three tickets in the same two minutes' implying possibly multiple tickets linked to one incident) — cardinality of the origin roles is not fully clarified beyond 'at least one of either'.

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate-of chains are stated as 'wrong' by intent (acyclic/direct-to-primary rule) but explicitly 'not enforced' in the system today. It's ambiguous whether the model should encode this as a hard constraint (which would misrepresent current real data, since 2-deep chains exist) or only as a documented business rule/aspiration.

source_references.excerpt: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.
